title: Mechanical behavior and stability of dispersed retained austenite in thermomechanically rolled and isothermally-treated TRIP-aided multiphase steel
abstract: The effect of thermomechanical processing and cooling conditions on the microstructure and mechanical properties during multi-step interrupted tensile tests was investigated in 0.24C–1.55Mn-0.87Si-0.40Al multiphase steel. Two temperature variants of isothermal bainitic holdings at 450 and 350 °C were applied. The tensile tests were interrupted at strain levels of 5, 10, 15%. The microstructure was assessed using light and SEM microscopy. EBSD analysis was performed to determine the retained austenite (RA) distribution and size. Detailed calculations concerning the mechanical performance were performed including the Jaoul-Crussard's analysis. Multiphase steels with the high retained austenite fraction (ca. 15%) of different γ phase sizes below 4 μm in a ferritic-bainitic matrix (with an average size of <6 μm) have been obtained. The research showed that during martensitic transformation of RA, the grain undergoes fragmentation. It has been shown that for the proper use of the TRIP effect, it is necessary to produce the dispersed RA of different sizes in the structure instead of striving for maximum fragmentation, which is a commonly used practice. Obtaining too small grains in the microstructure blocks their transformation during deformation due to their too high stability. Obtaining grains of one size leads to the intensification of the TRIP effect at a given stage of deformation only, reducing the plasticity in the others. The corresponding different mechanical stability of the γ phase ensures a gradual martensitic transformation and beneficial strain hardening progress.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The strain-induced martensitic transformation (SIMT) [ 1 ] is used to control the structure and mechanical properties of multi-phase structure steels intended for use in responsible structural elements of cars [ 2 ]. This is a reason of still high or even growing interest in all generations of Advanced High Strength Steels (AHSS) [ 3 ] showing a favorable combination of high mechanical properties and plasticity [ 4 ]. Their undeniable advantage over conventional low-alloy high-strength steels, as well as steels with a ferritic-martensitic microstructure (DP – dual phase), comes down to maintaining high plasticity despite increasing strength [ 5 ]. It results from the change of the steel phase composition (γ → α’) under conditions of increasing plastic deformation. The condition for obtaining high plasticity is the gradual transformation of the retained austenite (RA) into martensite (M) [ 6 ]. It prevents the localization of plastic deformation due to strong strain strengthening of the areas surrounding austenite grains or austenitic-bainitic (B-RA) islands [ 7 ], where the TRIP (TRansformation Induced Plasticity) effect occurs. The uniform distribution of dispersed RA ensures a gradual martensitic transformation in subsequent places of the sample. The high level of strain hardening [ 8 ] determines the delay of the neck formation, and thus obtaining high elongation of the steel. Moreover, replacing ductile RA with hard martensite can be compared to dispersion hardening, as well as to the characteristics of a composite material, in which particles of high hardness are homogeneously distributed in a ductile ferritic matrix. These complex factors determine the overall increase in the tensile strength of steel.

The problem of forming the structure of multi-phase steels produced by cold rolling and subsequent heat treatment has been well documented in the literature [ 9–11 ]. Annealing of the steel in the range between A c1  and A c3  does not pose any difficult problems, which allows a good control of the proportion of ferrite (F) and austenite being in equilibrium during the intercritical annealing. Significant factors determining the final structure of steel are temperature and time of isothermal bainite transformation [ 12 , 13 ]. In case of the hot rolling, a main problem is to ensure appropriate cooling conditions conducive to obtaining a desired fraction of ferrite with an appropriate morphology. It depends not only on the adaptation of the cooling conditions to the γ → α transformation but also on the hot-working, which determines the final structure of the prior austenite. Obtaining fine-grained polygonal ferrite of an appropriate proportion requires a controlled hot-rolling resulting in the gradual refinement of γ phase grains and the final structure of fine-grained, strongly pancaked austenite formed under conditions of limited recrystallization.

Most of the research on TRIP steels concerned materials isothermally treated after cold rolling [ 14 , 15 ]. The thermomechanical processing of Si–Al steels with Nb and Ti microadditions with the interaction of these factors under hot or cold deformation conditions has been studied to a much lesser extent. The effect of the finishing rolling temperature on microstructure refinement was investigated in works [ 16–18 ]. The influence of the conditions of plastic deformation and subsequent cooling on structural parameters of supercooled austenite transformation products was the subject of research by Skalova et al. [ 16 ] and Koh et al. [ 19 ]. They found that the lack of sufficient control of the finishing rolling conditions may lead to the formation of coarse-grained ferrite and/or bainite. A necessary condition for obtaining a multiphase structure with an appropriate proportion and morphology of individual structural constituents is to develop cooling conditions based on diagrams of supercooled austenite transformations [ 20 ]. The nucleation of ferrite after the hot-working was investigated in Refs. [ 17 , 19 ], whereas bainite in Refs. [ 14 , 21 ]. The effect of plastic deformation in TRIP steels on a C enrichment and the amount of retained austenite was investigated in Refs. [ 22 , 23 ]. The optimal selection of the thermomechanical processing parameters needs to be based on the DCCT diagrams [ 24 ], taking into account the austenite deformation prior to multi-step cooling, which best represents real process conditions. Meanwhile, many recent papers [ 25–27 ] skip the stage of plastic deformation process, which may limit the potential of the produced steels. The optimal use of the TRIP effect requires a gradual transformation of the RA into martensite associated with greater strain hardening rate during the entire straining process [ 28 ].

In the undertaken work, this goal was attempted to be achieved by improving the multi-phase structure of microalloyed Si–Al TRIP steel under thermomechanical treatment conditions. Particularly, the fragmentation, morphology, and distribution of RA affected by plastic deformation were taken into account. The influence of these treatments on the TRIP effect, austenite transformation, overall stability of RA, and thus the mechanical properties during deformation, were analyzed. The paper presents the complex evolution of the multiphase microstructure and mechanical properties as a function of the incremental strain level for thermomechanically processed Nb–Ti-microalloyed steel with silicon partially replaced by Al. The complex approach in linking microstructural features of these advanced multiphase microalloyed steels with mechanical behavior is a novelty of the study.

sections.heading: Material and processing route
paragraphs:
A 0.24C-0.87Si-0.40Al–NbTi TRIP steel with Si partially replaced by Al was used for the tests. The full chemical composition of the steel is presented in  Table 1 
                         .

The steel was designed to obtain a ferritic-bainitic microstructure with RA. It is characterized by increased contents of Mn, Si and Al. The carbon content was limited to 0.24% for proper weldability. At the same time, it allows for obtaining high strength properties and austenite's enrichment. Manganese acts as a RA stabilizer and decreases the temperature of cementite precipitation [ 29 ]. Silicon reduces the carbide precipitation during bainitic transformation increasing the RA fraction. However, Si has several significant drawbacks: it causes casting problems, deteriorates the quality of sheet surface during hot-rolling and affects negatively surface wettability by zinc during hot-dip galvanizing [ 30 ]. That's the reason why Si was partly replaced by Al, which doesn't cause these problems. Aluminum increases the carbon solubility in ferrite, and also limits the carbides precipitation [ 31 ]. The Ti and Nb microadditions were aimed to form carbides, nitrides and carbonitrides during hot-rolling.

The steel was melted in VSG-50 vacuum furnace by Balzers. The process was performed in argon atmosphere. After casting, a ⌀ 130 × 200 mm ingot was subsequently forged and roughly hot-rolled (temperature range: 1200-900 °C) to the plate thickness of 4.5 mm. The material on this stage was characterized by ferrite-pearlite microstructure with some small fraction of bainite and an average grain size of 25 μm. The occurrence of bainite proves the increased hardenability of steel.

The fundamental part of the microstructure and properties forming was thermomechanical processing schematically shown in  Fig. 1 
                         . First the material was reheated to 1100 °C for full austenization. Next the thickness of plate was reduced to 2 mm by hot-rolling in three passes (1050 °C, ε 1 -0.28; 950 °C, ε 2 -0.30; 850 °C, ε 3 -0.22). In order to obtain the high α phase pancaking degree, the finish temperature of the hot rolling was set to 850 °C. The cooling parameters were established basing on the previous investigations [ 20 ] concerning DCCT diagrams (deformation continuous cooling transformation). The study showed that both diagrams (CCT and DCCT diagrams) of the investigated steel show clear differences. The changes of phase transformation regions occurred especially for ferrite and pearlite areas. The beginning of ferritic transformation in case of deformed materials starts ten times faster compared to the non-deformed samples. Moreover, Ac 1  temperature is higher by 80 °C (in the highest point) in comparison to the undeformed material. The pearlitic transformation also starts much faster; moreover, the pearlitic start temperature also increases by almost 100 °C. The temperature (∼ 550 °C) and extent of bainitic transformation and M s  seem to be insensitive to deformation [ 20 ]. These differences must be taken into account during the design of heat treatment process, which is preceded by hot working.

The proposed heat treatment assumed cooling at a rate of 15 °C/s up to ∼730 °C, slow cooling of the material (2 °C/s for 50 s) after entering the ferritic transformation area (1st step of austenite stabilization), and quick cooling (40 °C/s) before entering the pearlitic field to avoid the formation of this phase. The next step was bainitic isothermal holding (IH) within 600 s allowing for obtaining a sufficient fraction of bainite to enrich the remaining austenite in carbon (2nd step of austenite stabilization). The isothermal holding was performed in two temperature variants: 350 and 450 °C, which should affect an amount of RA and morphologies of bainite and RA. The temperature parameters were selected as providing the high fraction of RA basing on the previous wider research on this topic described in Ref. [ 21 ]. After finishing the isothermal step, samples were air cooled to room temperature.

paragraphs:

The microstructures of near-neck areas (along the rolling and tensile direction) of thermomechanically processed and tensile tested samples were subsequently subjected to following tests: light and confocal microscopy using LSM Exciter 5 and scanning electron microscopy using Supra 25 by Zeiss. Microscopic observations were performed to characterize the microstructure and morphology of structural constituents. Samples for investigations were cut, grinded (220–1200 grid SiC papers) and polished (9, 3 and 1 μm paste) according to standard metallographic procedures [ 39 , 40 ]. Etching was performed in Nital and sodium metabisulfite reagent. Some samples were also subsequently etched in Klemm's reagent to make the different phases better identified in light microscopy.

Electron Back Scattering Diffraction (EBSD) was applied to determine the characteristics of RA. Sample preparation was finished by polishing using colloidal silica for 40 min. For the analysis, an acceleration voltage of 20 kV, tilt angle of 70°, working distance of 16 mm, and step size of 0.025 μm were used. X-ray diffraction (XRD) was performed using X'Pert Pro diffractometer to confirm the EBSD results and determine the amount of RA in the microstructure (using Rietveld method [ 41 , 42 ]). The determination of the RA fraction was performed according to Ref. [ 43 ], using HighScore Plus software (Version 3.0) containing a dedicated inorganic crystal structure database (PAN-ICSD) with the implemented Rietveld refinement module. The cobalt cathode (λKα = 0.179 nm) and the PIXcel 3D detector were used with the parameters of 40 kV and 30 mA. The diffraction lines were recorded in the Bragg–Brentano geometry in the angular scope of 45–105° (2θ), with the step of 0.026°. Basing on the X-ray diffractograms the austenite lattice parameters were calculated. It allows to determine a carbon content in the austenite, i.e., the most important factor influencing its thermodynamic stability [ 44 ]. sections.heading: Microstructure of thermomechanically rolled samples
paragraphs:
A different temperature of isothermal holding of steel in the bainitic region resulted in a little bit different microstructures presented in  Fig. 2 
                         . In case of IH450 sample ( Fig. 2 a,c) a fine-grained ferritic-bainitic structure with a ferrite fraction of about 60% and a large fraction of retained austenite was obtained. Retained austenite can be distinguished from ferrite by its shade and morphology; the latter is darker and shows a more rounded and spherical morphology, while the RA is light and has a sharp acicular shape. Martensite is more difficult to distinguish, but its presence is more coarse and shows a distinct submorphology, which is caused by stronger etching of this phase by nital [ 46 ].

The dark areas in the bainite islands show a neglectable fraction of pearlite ( Fig. 3 
                         ). The globular austenite grain adjacent to the pearlite is partially transformed due to the lower enrichment in carbon, whereas the smaller ones remain stable.

The average size of ferrite grains is about 6 μm. The RA is located at their boundaries in the form of irregular-blocky grains with a size up to 4 μm. A large part of RA is located in the bainite islands. The microstructure also contains martensite – the central areas of the biggest RA grains underwent martensitic transformation, which indicates a variation in thermal stability of RA. The analysis of the structures obtained from the SEM ( Fig. 2 c) confirms that the austenite often occurs between laths of bainitic ferrite as elongated, thin layers or fine grains with a size of about 1 μm. Some of the austenite grains present in the ferritic matrix are elongated in the rolling direction, which proves that they arose under conditions of high strain accumulation at a temperature lower than the end temperature of austenite recrystallization.

The appearance of small pearlite fraction in the microstructure is probably due to the acceleration of the pearlitic transformation as a result of lowering the deformation temperature to 850 °C and three-step deformation (compared to one-step deformation applied in the dilatometer). An additional influence on the acceleration of the supercooled austenite transformations could also have an increase in the strain rate from 1 (DCCT diagram was developed in dilatometric tests at 1 s −1  [ 20 ]) to about 10s −1 . This indicates a high dependence of austenite phase transformations on the conditions of the finishing hot working. The ferritic matrix grains are more elongated in the direction of rolling, and the pearlite is located in places, where under optimal conditions, there should be retained austenite - i.e., at ferrite grain boundaries or at ferrite-bainite interfaces.

Lowering the isothermal holding temperature in the bainitic range to 350 °C results in obtaining a ferritic-bainitic structure with a similar fraction of RA ( Fig. 2 b). This phase located in the boundary regions of bainitic islands is usually in the shape of grains up to 2 μm, whereas in the middle of the bainitic islands austenite occurs as thin, locally deformed layers located between the bainitic ferrite laths. A large part of RA located between the bainitic ferrite laths shows a character of continuous or interrupted layers with an average thickness of about 0.5 μm. In case of the IH350 sample, irregular RA grains with a small elongation in the direction of plastic flow, located mainly in the ferritic matrix, are dominating.

sections.heading: Mechanical stability of retained austenite
paragraphs:
Table 2 
                          presents RA characteristics of both thermomechanical processing variants. The fraction of RA in IH450 is 14.4% and a carbon content in this phase amounts to 1.14 wt%. For the IH350 sample the values are 15.1% and 1.23 wt%, respectively. In general, the average amount of retained austenite determined by the EBSD technique is in good agreement with the X-ray method (the discrepancy is less than 2%).

The M sγ  of IH450 sample, calculated on the basis of equation  (8)  in only a few degrees lower than the room temperature (10 °C). It is caused by some pearlite formation, which consumed carbon (cementite) to some extent and consequently lowered its content in the austenite. In case of IH350 sample, the lack of pearlite allows to obtain a higher C content in the austenite. That's why the calculated M sᵞ  temperature is lower (−28 °C).

Fig. 6 
                          presents EBSD results, which indicate the changes in a RA grain size with increasing strain. The microstructure of the samples in the initial state contains grains up to ∼4.5 μm for IH450 and ∼3.5 μm for IH350 samples. The distribution of grain size indicates the dominance of smaller grains but the ones bigger than 2 μm are 45% and 35%. Grains bigger than 3 μm are about 20% and 10%, respectively. Tensile deformation of the sample causes the SIMT starting from the biggest grains while the smallest ones remain stable. At the strain level of 10% in IH450 sample, the remaining RA grains larger than 2 μm are about 9% and larger than 3 μm are only ∼3%. The disappearance of large grains is clearly visible in the micrographs presented in  Fig. 6 a–c. The grains smaller than 1 μm are at a level of 23, 27 and 58% for strain levels of 0, 5 and 10%, respectively. In case of IH350 sample at 10% strain, the majority of the grains show a size lower than 1.5 μm. The IH350 sample shows the higher refinement at each deformation step. However, the proportional evolution of grain size with increasing strain is comparable.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs:
More detailed information on the steel strengthening can be obtained on the basis of the strain hardening exponent (n) changes ( Fig. 8 
                         ). In the initial range of deformation, it rises gradually reaching the maximum value of about 0.24 at a true strain of 0.08. The significantly higher increase of (n) in case of IH450 sample is related to the higher fraction of globular – less stable grains, which undergo the SIMT as first. The further continuous decrease together with a further strain increase to 0.14 indicates the contribution of the SIMT to the delay of the strain localization in the sample. After the strain 0.14, a more rapid decrease in the strain hardening exponent occurs but with a still high value of n = 0.2 at the true strain of 0.17 corresponding to the state immediately before the formation of the neck in the sample.

The true stress – true strain curve of IH350 sample is similar to the previous case at a little bit higher stress values over the entire deformation range. The value of the (n) exponent in the initial deformation stage gradually increases reaching a maximum of about 0.2 at a strain of 0.07. It is about 0.04 lower than that of H450 sample, which is due to more strengthened ferritic matrix resulting from the harder bainite straining effect. However, a favorable phenomenon is the maintenance of the work hardening exponent at a constant level until the true strain of about 0.14 ( Fig. 8 ). This proves the gradual transformation of the RA into martensite and the effective prevention of the strain concentration by the martensitic islands forming in subsequent areas of the samples. Despite the lower initial value of the strain hardening exponent - the more gradual progress of the martensitic transformation causes that immediately before the start of the neck formation, the values of (n) for both variants are similar. As a result, the gradual martensitic transformation favors the uniform elongation at the same level as IH450, but with a slightly higher UTS = 686 MPa and the UTS•UEl = 14,337 MPa ∙%.

Significant information on the behavior of steel under the conditions of tensile deformation is provided by the strain hardening rate curves ( Fig. 9 
                         ). A characteristic feature of all steels is a sudden drop in the strain hardening rate in the initial stage of deformation, which corresponds to the generation of new dislocations and the avoidance of obstacles by dislocations due to transverse slip [ 2 ]. However, multiphase steels are characterized by several times higher dσ/dε values compared to conventional deep-drawing steels due to the large portion of bainitic-austenitic islands [ 47 ].

Steel IH350 is characterized by greater strengthening in the range of strain to about 0.06. Despite the intense decrease in the strain hardening rate of the IH450 steel in the initial stage of deformation, the values of dσ/dε increase during the deformation in the range from 0.01 to 0.02 ( Fig. 9 ). This shape of the curves is often found in austenitic steels, where much larger amount of metastable austenite undergoes the martensitic transformation [ 2 ]. The initiation of the martensitic transformation and then its gradual progress determine the highest value of dσ/dε in the deformation range above approx. 0.06. In steel IH350, there is no increase in the strain hardening rate, but the smallest decrease in the value of dσ/dε in the final stage of deformation proves the most homogeneous contribution of the martensitic transformation to the increase of the strain hardening rate ( Fig. 9 ).

sections.heading: Effect of thermomechanical processing on the microstructure
paragraphs:
As it results from the previous research [ 20 ], the investigated Si–Al steel has a high A c3  temperature and a large difference between A c3  and A c1 . What is particularly important, the ferritic transformation starts relatively early, and the pearlitic region is delayed. Despite the advantageous shape of the ferritic bay, the amount of this phase in the case of non-deformed steels cooled at rates preventing the initiation of pearlitic transformation is negligible. The cooling of the steel after plastic deformation [ 20 ] from 850 °C has a beneficial effect on increasing the proportion of ferrite, with the simultaneous refinement of all structural constituents. The result of plastic deformation is the shift of the γ → α transformation to the shorter times with a simultaneous increase in the transformation start temperature. The disadvantageous effect of plastic deformation is some acceleration of the pearlitic transformation. The completion of hot deformation at the temperature of 850 °C resulted in obtaining a fine-grained structure of prior austenite ( Fig. 10 
                         ). The ferritic transformation under the conditions of the fine-grained structure of the prior austenite with an accumulated strain [ 48 , 49 ] resulted in fine-grained transformation products. The nucleation of ferrite in the plastically deformed austenite occurs simultaneously at the grain boundaries and twin boundaries and inside the grains in areas with high strain concentration [ 17 ]. The ferrite fraction was about 60% with an average grain diameter of about 6 μm. Further rapid cooling and IH of the steel led to the transformation of some austenite into bainitic ferrite, whereas austenite areas with the highest carbon enrichment, especially in the vicinity of fine-grained ferrite remained untransformed.

The fine-grained structure of austenite increases the total area of grain boundaries, leading to a high nucleation rate of bainitic ferrite [ 50 ]. However, the growth of plates under conditions of fine-grained structure is inhibited by austenite grain boundaries, which prevent the nucleation and growth of successive bainitic ferrite plates at the boundary of primary plates - as is the case for bainite formed in large austenite grains [ 51 ]. The kinetics of bainitic ferrite growth controlled only by the nucleation rate at the grain boundaries leads to a slow growth rate of the bainitic plates, which results in the preservation of a high fraction of RA. In the case of a low C concentration in the central areas of austenite caused by a long diffusion path, these regions transform into martensite during cooling to room temperature.

sections.heading: Effect of increasing tensile strain on mechanical properties
paragraphs: In the initial stage of plastic deformation (5% tensile strain), the central areas of the largest austenite grains located in the ferritic matrix are transformed. The determined M s  temperature ( Table 2 ) is the average value of all austenite grains of various sizes and morphology. Therefore, it may locally vary, assuming the highest M s  values for large, blocky grains situated in the ferritic matrix. The martensitic transformation of blocky RA grains is accompanied by a high value of the (n) exponent ( Fig. 8 ). The deformation increase to 10% preserves the martensitic transformation rate of smaller austenite grains located in ferrite, and the austenite grains located at the boundaries of ferrite and bainite. A large fraction of transformed austenite determines the maintenance of the strengthening exponent at a near constant level. A further increase in the deformation causes a significant elongation of the ferritic matrix grains. The deformation of the bainitic ferrite determines the initiation of the martensitic transformation in the layered areas of greater thickness austenite.

The summarized results of research on the SIMT of the RA at different strain levels, expressed by the mechanical stability parameter k 
                            γ 
                         , are shown in  Fig. 11 
                         . They base on the model of Sugimoto et al. [ 52 ]. The k 
                            γ 
                          value depends on the slope of the line representing the logarithmic change of the retained austenite fraction as a function of true strain. The RA in both variants shows high mechanical stability. The obtained k 
                            γ 
                          values (2.96 and 2.36 for IH450 and IH350 samples, respectively) in the investigated steel with Si partially replaced by Al are few times lower (k 
                            γ 
                         ∼10) than in case of 0.17C–1.4Si–2Mn silicon-added TRIP steel investigated in Ref. [ 53 ]. The lower k 
                            γ 
                          values mean the higher austenite stability. Sugimoto et al. [ 54 ] also reported the lower RA stability (k 
                            γ 
                         ∼2.7) in another 0.2C-1.5Mn-1.5Si silicon-added alloy than the one determined in the IH350 sample. Taking into account the comparable fractions and grain sizes of the RA ( Fig. 2 ) in the investigated steel, the difference in the mechanical stability of the RA results mainly from the different carbon content in this phase, amounting to 1.14 and 1.23% for IH450 and IH350 variants, respectively.

Fig. 12 
                          presents Jaoul-Crussard's curves [ 33 ] of the logarithmic change of the steel hardening rate as a function of strain. The work strengthening of the tested steels are divided into three stages: (1) deformation of the ferritic matrix; (2) inhibition of the decline in the strain hardening rate or its increase, which is the most characteristic for TRIP steels and is associated with lower ferrite deformation and the intense SIMT of the RA, mainly in the form of blocky grains; (3) and the SIMT of the RA, mainly in the form of small, irregular grains and layers located in bainitic islands. In both variants, a similar slope of the curves in the first hardening stage proves comparable ferrite hardening. The initiation of the 2nd stage takes place at different values of deformation. In the IH450 variant, a large fraction of blocky austenite grains effectively increases the strain hardening rate of the steel. The more gradual martensitic transformation of the retained austenite in the IH350 variant determines the lower marking of stage II in the curves shown in  Fig. 12 . The higher carbon content and the RA fraction in the form of layers located in the bainitic ferrite result in a slower decrease of the strain hardening rate in the last strengthening stage in the steel produced at lower isothermal holding temperature (IH350 variant).

The results indicate that grains with a larger diameter in the IH450 sample have a positive effect in the first stage of deformation. However, they account for a large part of RA, which reduces the strengthening in further stages. The IH350 sample with more variable grain sizes shows a better TRIP effect throughout the entire deformation region resulting in a higher strain level at fracture conditions.

The microstructure of the IH350 sample shows a slightly greater fragmentation of austenite resulting from a lower temperature of isothermal holding as well as the higher C enrichment in the austenite compared to IH450 sample. Despite the similar proportion of RA and its similar quantitative characteristics during the transformation, these factors increase the plasticity in relation to the IH450 sample. Mechanical properties of TRIP steels, apart from the contribution of the TRIP effect itself, are controlled by a matrix, the share of which is over 80%. Soft and hard phases have a direct impact on the plasticity and strength of the deformed alloy, which was reported in Ref. [ 55 ]. Yao et al. [ 56 ] indicated that lowering the baintic transformation temperature by 200 °C may decrease the bainitic plate thickness by over 30%, and increase the hardness by 15%. Hence, lowering the transformation temperature and thus bainite plate thickness is responsible for the strength increase. According to the literature [ 57 , 58 ], lowering the baintic transformation temperature affects the fragmentation of not only the ferritic bainite plates themselves but also the intralath RA. The greater stability of the RA resulting from its refinement and carbon enrichment are the major reasons of an ductility increase. As the results of strain hardening exponent ( Fig. 8 ) and strain hardening rate ( Fig. 9 ) show, in case of IH450 sample, there is a clear point of intense martensitic transformation due to the higher fraction of less stable RA. The sample with more refined RA presents more gradual deformation without the localized transformation of RA. Thus, despite obtaining similar microstructures, both the strength and plasticity of the IH350 sample are higher.

sections.heading: Martensite formation in the deformed TRIP steel
paragraphs: The stability and fraction of RA are a function of many factors depending on a chemical composition of steel, its structural condition, stress state and plastic deformation conditions. Numerous studies [ 59 , 60 ] have shown that the distribution of carbon concentration in austenite is heterogeneous and often changes even across the cross-section of individual grains. It was reported [ 59 ] that the optimal use of the SIMT can be obtained for the C content in the austenite ranging from 1 to 1.8% by mass. The RA present between the polygonal ferrite grains has a lower C content compared to the γ-phase regions located in bainitic islands [ 61 ]. The reason for this is the lack of carbon enrichment of the first type of grains during the bainitic transformation. On the other hand, the austenite regions located at the interfacial boundaries of polygonal ferrite/bainite may have a variable carbon content - depending on an adjacent structural constituent. The next important factors are size and morphology of RA. The size of the RA grains located at the grain boundaries of the ferritic matrix or the ferrite/bainite interfaces is most often from 1 to 5 μm [ 62 ], whereas layers located between the bainitic ferrite plates have a width from 0.01 to 0.8 μm. Wang and van der Zwaag [ 63 ] showed that apart from enriching austenite with carbon, a significant factor for its stabilization is the reduction of RA grain size, which significantly increases the number of nuclides needed to obtain a specific martensite fraction. This is due to the effect of austenite grain boundaries, at which the growth of martensite plates stops. This means that the refined RA grains require an increase in the driving force to start the SIMT, reflected by a decrease in the M s  temperature. Moreover, the nature of matrix also affects the stability. High-strength phases as bainite or martensite not only increase strength of material but also introduce hydrostatic pressure [ 64 ] counteracting the increase in the volume of martensite during the transformation, resulting in an increase in the RA stability. The crystallographic texture also significantly affects mechanical properties of TRIP steels. Emadoddin et al. [ 65 ] observed significant defferences in RA stability depending on the straining direction. Chen et al. [ 26 ] showed that stretching in rolling direction leads to higher elongation which is caused by more intensive TRIP efect, compared to the one obtained during stretching in tranverse direction.

As it is rather difficult to say that the SEM and EBSD results presented earlier can represent the entire microstructure (due to the small area), IH450 steel samples for the initial state and 5% tensile strain were etched in Klemm's reagent ( Fig. 13 
                         ). In case of proper application, it allows to differentiate the individual phases based on their colors. The influence of etching time using Klemm's reagent is visible in  Fig. 13 a. The result of the etching was the coloring the ferrite and bainite to beige, martensite to blue/navy blue, whereas austenite remained white due to its low susceptibility to Klemm's reagent. The increase of martensite fraction as a function of strain is now clearly visible in a much larger scale. What's more, etching also revealed that most of the martensite was formed by partial transformation of the biggest RA grains. There are no totally transformed grains visible. The martensitic transformation also occurred in fine grains but to a much smaller extent. It is visible that the formed martensite causes “fragmentation” of initial RA grains ( Fig. 6 ).

Taking into account the above microstructural and mechanical properties results, for both variants it is a clear pattern of SIMT starting from the largest grains and progressing to smaller grains ( Fig. 14 
                         ). The analysis of the strengthening behavior shows that the martensitic transformation of large grains in the initial stage of deformation is beneficial. However, in the case of only coarse-grained RA, the TRIP effect wears off quickly and the sample is fractured. On the other hand, when the material exhibits ultra-fine-grained RA, the TRIP effect is not active in the initial stage of deformation, causing a reduction in strength and plasticity. Moreover, as the research has shown, the smallest grains do not transform even at maximum deformation [ 66 , 67 ]. Taking these factors into account, the most appropriate seems to produce microstructures with a different grain size of the RA without any dominance of particular size. This allows to utilize the TRIP effect at the same level throughout the entire deformation process ensuring maximum strength and ductility.

Obtaining the effect of the intended distribution of grain size is not a simple issue and may require complex approach. Grain size control is achieved through the use of microadditions, commonly applied in High-Strength Low Alloy (HSLA) steels [ 4 , 68 ]. Another method is to modify a rate of both heating and cooling of the material and the temperature of individual processes. In Ref. [ 55 ] the authors indicated that shortening of the isothermal holding step followed by fast cooling may lead to homogeneous carbon distribution in the RA grains, which also influence more random transformation sequence. Another, less used phenomenon among the 1st generation AHSS steels is the Austenite Reverse Transformation (ART) process [ 69 , 70 ]. The ART is based on the nucleation and growth of austenite in a martensitic matrix. Nucleation takes place at the border of the martesitic plates and at the junction points of the 3 plates. It is characterized by obtaining austenite with a lamellar morphology and a grain size depending on the initial martensite morphology. Attempts to control a size of the final RA can be made by adjusting the starting structure, e.g. by a partial ART process. These are only preliminary assumptions, which nevertheless show further research potential in TRIP-aided multiphase steels.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
The work concerns a detailed study of thermomechanical processing and resulting mechanical properties as well as microstructure evolution of the microalloyed TRIP steel with Si partially replaced by Al investigated at different strain levels. Thermomechanical processing considering isothermal holding steps at 450 and 350 °C allows to obtain multiphase steels with a high RA fraction (∼ 15%) of different sizes. The UTS at the level over 663 MPa with the reasonable ductility (TEl ∼ 24%) were obtained. It has been shown that for the proper use of the TRIP effect, it is necessary to produce dispersed RA of different sizes in the structure instead of striving for maximum fragmentation. The main findings of the present study are as follows: 
                         
                            • 
                            The martensitic transformation begins in the central areas of the blocky RA grains located in the ferritic matrix causing their gradual fragmentation. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            The research showed the necessity to obtain the RA grains of various sizes (from 4 to 1 μm) in order to ensure a continuous TRIP effect throughout the entire strain range. Grains smaller than 1 μm are too stable or are very difficult to transform, which resulted in the lack of their contribution to the TRIP effect. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            The fine-grained ferrite and gradually transforming RA grains of 4–1 μm diameter maintained the work hardening exponent at the level above 0.2 in a wide strain range. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            The obtained fine-grained multiphase mixture provided 3-step hardening behavior with the most beneficial stage II corresponding to the SIMT of fragmented, blocky RA grains. The refinement of all structural constituents resulted in the relatively stable RA expressed by the mechanical stability parameter at a level of kγ ∼2.9 and 2.3 for the steels isothermally held at 450 and 350 °C, respectively.
